1.pericope_label: Every man by his own standard, with the ensign of his father's house

schools.summary: Give the reader everything the learned have assembled, then tell him what it is worth. Set out the Talmudists on the ensigns down to the last device, an ass for Issachar, a ship for Zebulun, a handful of corn for Asher; lay before him a full reconstructed plan of the camp with the ground allotted tribe by tribe in square cubits and a total of a little more than twelve square miles; compare the ranks of the Israelite host with the descending scale of command in a modern army. Then withdraw the authority of all of it in your own person. Scripture says which tribes held which quarter and no more; how they stood individually cannot be pretended to, and to claim minute exactness in such a case would be absurd. What the plan is good for is a general idea of how the thing probably was, and the reason for confidence is not the reconstruction but its author: the arrangement was God's, and therefore in every respect what it ought to be for the comfort and safety of that multitude. Then read the three concentric camps -- the Lord, the Levites, the people -- as answering to the holy of holies, the holy place and the outer court. On the distance keep both reasons in view, reverence and caution, since nearness might tempt them to approach what was not theirs, and put the space at two thousand cubits.

Read the arrangement as a remedy, and name the disease. So natural is ambition to man that without an assigned position they would have quarrelled for the place of honour. Reuben's house would have found it grievous to resign the firstborn's dignity; the sons of the handmaids would not have granted that Leah's and Rachel's children should always precede them; every tribe would have claimed rank in proportion to its numbers; and the splitting of Joseph into two required divine authority, since Manasseh, superior by the law of nature, would never have consented to follow his younger brother. God stopped all of it at once by so arranging their ranks that each one knew his own band. Mark what kind of rule this was. The sole will of God was more than sufficient to prevent every quarrel, but He chose to govern generously and paternally rather than despotically, and so conformed Himself to their wishes rather than driving them by compulsion. Then fix the occasion plainly: the order comes after the numbering, as the congregation was about to set forward, and governs both the camp and the march.

Take the encampment as a picture of the reader's own condition before taking it as history. They dwelt in tents and carried them wherever they went, finding no city to dwell in; that is a movable state and a military one, and while we pitch in this world we should be pressing through it. From the tribes camping together draw the duty of keeping up affection and communion among relations; from the fixed quarters, that it is God who appoints the bounds of our habitation, and that we must not love to flit. On the standards themselves be honest that it is uncertain, and give the conjectures without choosing between them: colours matching the stones of the ephod, or arms drawn from Jacob's blessing, or the four chief ensigns of lion, man, ox and eagle that would make Ezekiel's vision allude to them. Then set the tabernacle in the centre like a general's pavilion and get two things from it, that God in the midst was their comfort and that the sanctuary was their charge, since no invader could reach it without breaking through their thickest squadrons. Last, press the change: they were ordered to pitch afar off, and we are invited to draw near and come boldly.

State the order and the numbers, and let the consequence carry the weight. The standard of Judah encamped in front, toward the east, with Issachar and Zebulun at its side, all of them descendants of Leah, under Judah's command and banner; the division amounted to a hundred and eighty-six thousand four hundred men, and it was to march out first when the camp broke up. Draw from that arrangement the one inference the text supports and stop there: Judah led the way as the champion of his brethren, which is what Jacob's blessing had said of him. Do not moralize the position and do not reconstruct the ground plan; the descent of the tribes and the order of march are what the passage gives, and they are enough to show why this tribe stood where it stood.

debates.question: What did the standards look like?

sides.position: Uncertain, and three conjectures are worth reporting without choosing between them: colours matching the stones of the ephod, arms drawn from Jacob's blessing, or four chief ensigns of lion, man, ox and eagle that would make Ezekiel's vision allude to them
Four great ensigns distinguished by colours or figures, with further particular ensigns belonging to the several fathers' houses beneath them

The Talmudists give a device for every tribe, an ass for Issachar, a ship for Zebulun, a handful of corn for Asher and the rest; but how the camp was arranged individually cannot be pretended to, and to claim minute exactness would be absurd

debates.question: Why did God assign the places himself?

sides.position: To forestall specific quarrels: Reuben's house resigning the firstborn's dignity, the handmaids' sons resenting perpetual inferiority, tribes claiming rank by numbers, and Manasseh refusing to follow a younger brother
To keep kin together, so that the younger sons of Leah served under Judah, Gad filled Levi's room beside Reuben, Rachel's posterity formed the third standard and Bilhah's eldest led the fourth
To place the sanctuary at the centre, where it was both the comfort of the whole camp and the charge no invader could reach without breaking through their thickest squadrons

outliers.note: Alone reproduces an entire reconstructed plan of the camp, with the ground allotted to each tribe in square cubits and a total of a little more than twelve square miles, and alone then withdraws its authority in his own person, saying that the text gives the quarters and no more and that to pretend to minute exactness would be absurd.

Alone presses the contrast between the arrangement and the reader's own standing, that Israel was ordered to pitch afar off in reverence and lest familiarity breed contempt, while we are not so ordered but invited to draw near and come boldly.

themes: Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house
far off about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch
the LORD spake unto Moses and unto Aaron, saying

3.pericope_label: The east side: Judah, Issachar and Zebulun set forth first

schools.summary: Ask who else could have assigned the places, and let the answer settle the doctrine. Left to themselves the tribes would have quarrelled over precedence as the disciples did over which should be greatest, since every one of them had a pretence to be first or at least not to be last; had Moses decided it they would have charged him with partiality. God does it, being himself the fountain and judge of honour, and in his appointment all must acquiesce. Turn that on the hearer at once: where providence has fixed our place we should be as satisfied as if a voice out of the tabernacle had assigned it, and where the choice is ours we have the rules not to sit down in the highest room and that whoever will be chief must be servant. On the captains, resist the levelling inference. That we are all children of one Adam does not abolish distinctions of place, since even among the children of the same Jacob God appointed one to be captain over the rest. Then make the princes' names do historical work: most of them carry God's name, and from that conclude that Israel in Egypt had not forgotten it but preserved it in their children's names and comforted themselves with it in affliction.

Answer the question of precedence in one stroke and let it stand. Judah held the first post and led the van on the march, not only because the tribe was the most numerous but chiefly because Christ, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, was to descend from it, and from the loins of Nahshon, the very man here named its chief captain. Say it briefly and do not multiply the application; the weight is in the identification itself, and a hearer who takes it will supply the rest.

Work at the level of the words and the ground before working at the level of the lesson. Note from Jarchi that the east is called what is before, as the west is called what is behind, so that the orientation of the camp is built into the Hebrew for the directions. Correct the picture the English order suggests: the three tribes did not stand in file with Judah first, but Judah lay between the other two, Issachar behind and Zebulun before, one on each side of the standard. Explain the contentment of the arrangement from the family: Issachar and Zebulun were Leah's youngest sons and Judah's own brothers, so they pitched under their elder brother without reluctance. And keep the small observations that show the record is exact -- that twenty days passed between the numbering and the setting forward in which not one of those counted died, so that the totals repeated here still stood precisely as they had been taken.

Attend to the recurring formula rather than to the persons. The phrase that carries each tribe's figure, his host and those that were numbered of them, means the army reckoned according to its mustered men, and it is the same phrase throughout; once that is settled the run of verses is a single construction repeated, not a series of separate statements. Give the totals as they stand and let the repetition itself show the regularity of the arrangement.

debates.question: Why was Judah given the first place?

sides.position: Not chiefly for its numbers but because Christ, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, was to descend from it, and from the loins of Nahshon, the man here named its captain and reckoned among Christ's ancestors, so that Christ in effect went before the camp
Because Judah led the way as the champion of his brethren, which is what Jacob's blessing had said of him, and his division marched out first when the camp broke up
Because Issachar and Zebulun were Leah's youngest sons and Judah's own brothers, so they pitched under their elder brother without reluctance

debates.question: How were the three eastern tribes actually placed?

sides.position: Not in file with Judah first, but Judah between the other two, Issachar behind and Zebulun before, one on each side of the standard
Issachar and Zebulun at Judah's side, under his command and banner, as a single division of a hundred and eighty-six thousand four hundred

outliers.note: Alone turns the princes' names into historical evidence, observing that most of them carry God's name at one end or the other and concluding that Israel in Egypt had not forgotten it, but preserved the remembrance of it in their children's names and comforted themselves with it in their affliction.

Alone corrects the arrangement the English order suggests, showing that the three eastern tribes did not stand in file but that Judah lay between the other two with the standard in the middle, and alone reports Aben Ezra's observation that not one of those numbered died in the twenty days before they set forward.

themes: on the east side toward the rising of the sun shall they of the standard of the camp of Judah pitch
Nahshon the son of Amminadab shall be captain of the children of Judah
All that were numbered in the camp of Judah... These shall first set forth

10.pericope_label: The south side: Reuben, Simeon and Gad; the tabernacle in the midst

schools.summary: Show, tribe by tribe, why no quarrel could arise in this camp, and ground each step in the family history. Simeon pitches under Reuben's standard because the two were brothers by the mother's side as well as the father's, so they might well be thought to agree; and because Reuben was not merely the elder of the two but the eldest of all Jacob's sons, Simeon would not grudge it. Gad stands on the opposite side of the standard, which fixes the arrangement on the ground with Reuben before and Simeon behind. Gad's own place rests on his birth twice over: as eldest son of Leah's handmaid Zilpah he is fitly set under Leah's firstborn, and as a handmaid's son he could not object to his situation. Keep host and camp distinct throughout, the host of Reuben being only a part of the camp that bears his name. And do not neglect the flags: Reuben's stone the sardius, his flag red with mandrakes; Simeon's the topaz, his flag green with Shechem; Gad's the agate, his flag neither black nor white but mixed, with a camp figured on it. Give the orientation too, that the south is the right hand, and that this was the right wing of the whole army.

Where a phrase invites an obvious reading, test it against the rest of the narrative before accepting it. That the tabernacle set forward in the midst is not to be understood strictly but largely, because on the march the tribe was divided, part of it going next after Judah and only the other part standing exactly in the centre of the camp. Make the correction briefly and without dispute; the point is that the arrangement described here and the order of march recorded later must be read together, and neither should be pressed into a precision the text does not claim.

Give the grouping and the descent that accounts for it: the standard of Reuben on the south, with Simeon and Gad, sprung from Leah and from Leah's maid Zilpah, associated with it and subordinated to it. Then attend to the names as textual data. Where the father of the captain of Gad is given here in a form that does not agree with the form used of the same man in the first chapter and again in the seventh, say so plainly and register the discrepancy rather than harmonizing it silently.

debates.question: How strictly is the tabernacle's place in the midst to be taken?

sides.position: Not strictly but largely, since on the march the tribe was divided, part going next after Judah and only the other part standing exactly in the centre
Strictly enough to be measured: the camp of the Levites reached four miles, the same extent given for Judah's

debates.question: Why could Reuben's camp be arranged without resentment?

sides.position: Because of the family ties at every step: Simeon a brother by the mother's side under the eldest of all Jacob's sons, and Gad both the eldest son of Leah's handmaid and, as a handmaid's son, in no position to object
Because Simeon and Gad were descendants of Leah and of Leah's maid Zilpah, and so were associated with Reuben's standard and subordinated to it

outliers.note: Alone questions whether the tabernacle's place in the midst is to be pressed, answering that it is not to be understood strictly but largely, since on the march the tribe was divided and only part of it stood in the centre.

Alone treats the captains' names as textual data, registering that the father of the captain of Gad is given here in a form that does not agree with the form used of the same man in the first and seventh chapters.

themes: On the south side shall be the standard of the camp of Reuben according to their armies
Then the tribe of Gad: and the captain of the sons of Gad shall be Eliasaph
Then the tabernacle of the congregation shall set forward with the camp of the Levites in the midst of the camp

18.pericope_label: The west side: Ephraim preferred before Manasseh; Benjamin

schools.summary: Take the inversion of birth order head on and show that nobody in this camp had grounds to complain. Manasseh, though the elder, was given no standard and was directed to pitch by his younger brother's; but since this agreed with Jacob's prophecy it could not well be objected to. Benjamin was Joseph's own younger brother, and being placed under the standard of a son of Joseph who stood in his father's room, he could not be offended. All three were Rachel's descendants, so they might well be thought to agree together and be content with their situation. Fix the arrangement on the ground as in the other camps: Benjamin under Ephraim's standard on the side opposite Manasseh, one before and one behind with the standard between, and the whole extending four miles. Report the flags -- Joseph's stone the onyx or sardonyx, his flag very black with Egypt figured on it because the two princes were born there, an ox for Ephraim and a unicorn for Manasseh, and Benjamin's jasper with a flag of twelve colours and a wolf. Then give the total plainly, the smallest of the four camps and nearly eighty thousand fewer than Judah's, without softening the contrast with the precedence just granted.

Answer the difficulty in a single clause and move on. Ephraim is here preferred before his brother according to the prophecy Jacob made when he crossed his hands over Joseph's sons. Nothing more is needed: the precedence is not explained by numbers, by merit or by any circumstance of the wilderness, but by a word spoken over the two boys long before, and naming that word is the whole of the exposition.

State the division and its place in the order. On the west stood the standard of Ephraim with Manasseh and Benjamin, that is to say the whole of the descendants of Rachel, a hundred and eight thousand one hundred men, forming the third division of the army and going forward in the third rank. Add nothing to it. Where the source verses are simply the muster repeated, the commentator's task is to identify the grouping and the sequence, not to supply reflection the text does not carry.

debates.question: On what ground was Ephraim set above Manasseh?

sides.position: On the prophecy Jacob made over Joseph's sons, and on nothing else
On the same prophecy, which is why it could not well be objected to; and Benjamin could not be offended either, being placed under the standard of a son of Joseph who stood in his father's room
The question is not raised; the western standard is simply the whole of Rachel's descendants, the third division of the army

outliers.note: Alone carries the catalogue of flags through this camp, giving Joseph's stone as the onyx or sardonyx with Egypt figured on a very black flag because the two princes were born there, an ox for Ephraim and a unicorn for Manasseh, and for Benjamin a jasper with a flag of twelve colours bearing a wolf.

themes: On the west side shall be the standard of the camp of Ephraim according to their armies
And by him shall be the tribe of Manasseh
All that were numbered of the camp of Ephraim... they shall go forward in the third rank

25.pericope_label: The north side: Dan hindmost; the sum of the camps; so they did

schools.summary: Explain first why a handmaid's son should have a standard at all, and give the reasons together: Dan was the firstborn of the sons of the handmaids, his tribe was warlike, and it was very numerous. The two placed with him could not object, being handmaids' sons themselves, Naphtali his younger brother by the mother's side as well as the father's and Asher the second son of Zilpah. Place the camp to the left of the tabernacle as the left wing of the army, four miles in extent, and record the flags: Dan's stone the ligure, his flag like a sapphire with a serpent; Asher's the beryl, his flag like the stone women adorn themselves with, an olive tree on it; Naphtali's the amethyst, his flag like clear wine whose redness is not strong, a hind on it. Then treat the closing verses as narrative and say what obedience actually consisted of -- forming into camps, appointing a captain over each tribe, erecting a standard to each camp, pitching every man by the standard he belonged to, and marching in that order, families under tribes and lesser houses under families. Note that the Levites were counted separately because they were a camp of themselves.

Ask why this camp was posted where it was, and answer in tactical terms rather than genealogical. Dan's was the strongest camp after Judah's, and therefore it came in the rear as Judah marched in the front, so that the tabernacle should be best guarded at the point where the danger was greatest. That is the whole observation, and it is worth making because the rest of the chapter accounts for position by descent; here the reason is the safety of the thing being carried.

Settle the wording before drawing conclusions from it. The closing formula for this camp, that they shall go hindmost with their standards, uses a phrase equivalent to the one used of the three earlier camps, according to their hosts, and means in each case the hosts of which the camp consisted; so the last division is not described differently from the others, only worded differently. Give the whole number, six hundred and three thousand five hundred and fifty, apart from the Levites. Then classify the final verse rather than expounding it: the statement that the children of Israel did as the Lord commanded is an anticipatory notice of what was carried out later, of the same kind as the closing remarks in Exodus about the passover and the setting up of the tabernacle.

debates.question: Why was Dan's camp placed last in the order of march?

sides.position: For defence: it was the strongest camp after Judah's, so it came in the rear as Judah marched in the front, that the tabernacle might be best guarded where the danger was greatest
By descent and precedence: Dan was firstborn of the handmaids' sons, his tribe warlike and very numerous, and the two placed with him were handmaids' sons who could not object

debates.question: What kind of statement is the closing verse?

sides.position: An anticipatory notice of what was carried out later, of the same kind as the closing remarks in Exodus about the passover and the setting up of the tabernacle

A record of what was actually done, to be filled out in detail: forming into camps, appointing captains, erecting standards, pitching by them and marching in that order on the twentieth day of the month

outliers.note: Alone accounts for a camp's position by tactics rather than by descent, making Dan the rearguard because his was the strongest camp after Judah's and the tabernacle needed guarding where the danger was greatest.

Alone settles the closing formula philologically, showing that according to their standards is equivalent to the according to their hosts used of the earlier camps, so that the last division is not described differently from the others but only worded differently.

themes: The standard of the camp of Dan shall be on the north side by their armies
All they that were numbered in the camp of Dan... They shall go hindmost with their standards
the children of Israel did according to all that the LORD commanded Moses
